All House Rules

House rules

Berry Rules

To overcome the fact that normal animals and pets do not get stronger as your character does, Berry Rules makes sure that pets that serve no purpose in combat will not be targeted by any attack (even AOE spells like Fireball). This does not protect animals that scale with your level, familiars, summons, or anything similar. If you have a pet do anything that would put them at risk, they can now be targeted by hostile creatures.

Bleeding Condition

A bleeding creature takes damage equal to its proficiency bonus at the start of its turn. It also has disadvantage on Strength, Dexterity, and Constitution ability checks and saving throws. It is removed by regaining hit points or by a creature making a successful Medicine check (DC 10 or half the damage taken, whichever is higher) as an action.

Casting Levelled Spells

You can not cast more than one spell that is level 3 or higher in a single turn, unless you have an additional action, such as from the Action Surge feature, or one of the spell’s casting time is a reaction.

Critical Rolls

A Natural (meaning just the value shown on the dice) 20 or a Natural 1 are Critical Successes and Critical Failures respectively. When landing a critical success on an attack, you roll the damage of the attack as normal, then double it at the end. You do the same for any additional damage the attack may do, such as Divine Smite or Booming Blade. A critical failure on an attack will always miss.

However, landing a NAT 20 or NAT 1 outside of attacking rolls usually means you perform either the best possible (and perhaps slightly better) outcome or the worst possible outcome respectively.

Examples:

  • Even if you roll a NAT 20 trying to fly and jump off a cliff, you won’t fly. You’ll be carried by a freak wind and land with minor scratches.
  • Even if you roll a NAT 1 trying to pet a dog, the worst that will happen is you step on its tail.
Dazed Condition

A dazed creature has their movement speed halved. On its turn, it can use either an action or a bonus action, not both, nor can it use reactions. The creature has disadvantage on attack rolls and other creatures have advantage on attack rolls against it.

Drinking a Potion

You can drink a potion (or similar brew) as a Bonus Action.

Finishing Blows

Whenever your character lands the final blow on the last enemy in combat, you may do a description of how you eliminate them. This can involve processes that usually amount to death.

Flanking (Surrounding)

When making a melee attack against a creature, you gain a +1 bonus to the To Hit roll for every other allied creature within 5 ft. of the target.

Variant Rule: Grouped Initiative

In this system, creatures act in Initiative Groups rather than on individual Initiative counts.

Step 1: Roll Group Initiative

When Initiative is called, each creature rolls a die based on the number of player characters in the party:

  • 1-3 characters: 1 group
  • 1–6 characters: 1d4, 2 groups
  • 7–9 characters: 1d6, 3 groups
  • 10–12 characters: 1d8, 4 groups
  • 13 or more characters: 1d10, 5 groups

Divide the result in half, rounding up. The final number determines which Initiative Group the creature belongs to (for example, rolling a 5 on a d8 places the creature in Group 3).

Step 2: Initiative Modifier and Rerolls

A creature’s Initiative modifier grants rerolls of its Group die:

  • For every +2 bonus to Initiative rolls, the creature may reroll once.
  • A +0 or +1 modifier grants no rerolls.
  • A +2 or +3 grants 1 reroll.
  • A +4 or +5 grants 2 rerolls, and so on.

Each reroll must be kept, even if it results in a lower group number.

Step 3: Divide by Side

Each Initiative Group is divided into two sides: players and enemies. A neutral or unaffiliated creature is treated as part of the enemies’ side.

Step 4: Determine Side Order

If both sides are present in the same Initiative Group, each side chooses a representative creature to make an Initiative check. Compare the results for each paired contest, then count victories. The side with the most victories acts first in that group. If the contest is tied, the players act first. If only one side is present in the group, no contest is made.

Step 5: Resolve the Round

Combat begins with the highest numbered Initiative Group that contains creatures. Within that group, the winning side acts first. All creatures on that side may act in any order they choose, one at a time. When that side has finished, the opposing side in the same group takes their turns in the same way. Combat then proceeds to the next lowest Initiative Group, continuing until all groups have acted. At the end of the round, combat returns to the highest Initiative Group.

Step 6: Abilities by Group

Any ability that refers to a specific Initiative count instead refers to Initiative Groups:

  • A lair action that occurs on Initiative count 20 instead occurs before the highest Initiative Group.
  • A lair action that occurs on Initiative count 1 instead occurs before the lowest Initiative Group.

Turn Order Within a Side

Creatures do not act simultaneously. One creature must complete its turn before another begins, though allies on the same side may freely decide the order in which they act.

Hiding in Plain Sight

When making a Dexterity (Stealth) check to hide, if the creature(s) you are attempting to hide from are able to clearly see you without any cover or concealment, you have a -10 deduction to your roll. If at any point you are Hidden and end your turn Hiding in Plain Sight, you must make another Dexterity (Stealth) check with the deduction. You can not Hide in Plain Sight while within 5 ft. of a creature that can see or hear you. Creatures have advantage on Wisdom (Perception) checks made to find you while you are Hiding in Plain sight.

Focus Techniques

In general, martial (non-magical) classes like the Fighter, Monk, or Barbarian tend to fall behind at mid-high levels. This disparity is usually caused by the intense utility that a spellcaster has coupled with the fact that most DMs (and I) do not throw multiple combats at the players in a single day, allowing spellcasters to Long Rest and replenish their precious Spell Slots more often. These techniques are abilities that help boost martial classes to be more in line with spellcasters.

Every 3rd level, Martial characters (every 6th level for half-casters such as Paladin and ranger) may choose a Focus technique from the list found here Phoenix’s Book of Bullshit. A focus technique may only be chosen once and you can only take a focus technique from a class’ list if you have levels in that class.

Variant Rule: Heroic Inspiration

You can be given Heroic Inspiration by the DM for doing something particularly interesting or in character, or by succeeding a Roll with Heroism. You can have a maximum of three Heroic Inspiration at once, though you lose all but one at the end of a session. If you have Heroic Inspiration, you can expend it any of the following ways:

  • When making an ability check, saving throw, or attack roll, you may choose to reroll the die, taking the higher result. This must be done before knowing the outcome of the roll.
  • When an ally you can see within 15 ft. fails a saving throw, you may choose to reroll their die as a reaction, taking the higher result. An ally may only benefit from this once per saving throw.
  • When you start your turn and are Incapacitated, you may choose to take an action but gain a level of exhaustion.
Rolling with Heroism

When attempting an ability check, saving throw, or attack roll, a character may declare a Roll with Heroism, and then describe how they break the bounds of normalcy and step into the extraordinary. A character may describe how they strike out at a creatures eyes to blind it, inspire a group of enemies to join their side, or scale up to the back of a raging dragon. If the DM accepts their description, they may then Roll with Heroism, with a DC higher than normal. On a success, the character gains more than what a normal success would elicit and are also awarded with a Heroic Inspiration. On a failure, the character suffers a consequence beyond what a normal failure would elicit.

If a character attempts to perform an action that is particularly cinematic, difficult, and interesting, the DM can make the check a Roll with Heroism. A Roll with Heroism made in this way allows the character to use abilities that allow them to reroll the die, except for Heroic Inspiration.

Item Crafting

Requirements: To make most items, you must have proficiency in an artisan’s tools. You must also have the required item supplies to craft an item. Each rarity of item has a different cost, shown as a GP amount worth of supplies required. At most magic shops or sometimes others like herbalists, jewelers, and smiths, you can purchase item supplies directly with GP. Likewise, you may also forage in certain places to acquire supplies. Each item rarity has an established DC, which you will roll against throughout the brewing.

Process: You must have an actual artisan’s tools to begin crafting an item, with the required supply cost immediately on hand. Once the crafting has started, the supplies are consumed and you must make a Arcana check against the rarity’s DC. If someone else with proficiency in Arcana or the same artisan’s tools is helping you, you may roll with advantage. For certain items, you may need to make a different skill check than Arcana. Once begun, you will have to roll this same check several more times before the crafting has completed. When the item is completed, if you rolled more failures than successes, then the item becomes unusable.

Time: The crafting progress can be paused and resumed at a later time. Each rarity specifies the minimum amount of time it takes before the item can be completed. It also specifies how many separate work periods you must spend to craft the item and how long each work period must be for the interaction to count. For each work period, you must make another check against the rarity’s DC. You may only perform one work period per day.

  • Common: 3 Days (3, 1 hr)
  • Uncommon: 1 Week (7, 2 hrs)
  • Rare: 3 Weeks (21, 3 hrs)
  • Very Rare: 3 Months (24, 4 hrs)
  • Legendary: 1 Year (36, 6 hrs)

Cost: Every item requires some amount of supplies, with its rarity corresponding to the cost.

  • Common: 15 GP
  • Uncommon: 40 GP
  • Rare: 100 GP
  • Very Rare: 450 GP
  • Legendary: 1500 GP

DC: Every item has a DC that you must roll a Arcana check (with Alchemist Supplies), adding your proficiency to the roll (doubled if expertise), against.

  • Common: DC 13
  • Uncommon: DC 15
  • Rare: DC 18
  • Very Rare: DC 20
  • Legendary: DC 25

Learning how to make a item: Every item has some amount of studying that needs to be done in order to create it, even if you are copying instructions from a written source. The amount of time is doubled if you are researching the item rather than receiving instructions.

  • Common: 6 hours
  • Uncommon: 12 hours
  • Rare: 24 hours
  • Very Rare: 72 hours
  • Legendary: 192 hours
Potion Making

Requirements: To make most potions or chemical mixtures, you must have proficiency in Alchemist’s Tools or an Herbalism Kit. You must also have the required potion supplies to brew a potion. Each rarity of potion has a different cost, shown as a GP amount worth of supplies required. At most herbalists or sometimes even general stores, you can purchase potion supplies directly with GP. Likewise, you may also forage in certain places to acquire supplies. Each potion rarity has an established DC, which you will roll against throughout the brewing.

Process: You must have an actual Herbalism Kit or Alchemist’s Tools to begin brewing a potion, with the required supply cost immediately on hand. Once the brewing has started, the supplies are consumed and you must make a Arcana check (with Alchemist Supplies) or a Nature Check (with Herbalism Kit), adding your proficiency to the roll (doubled if expertise), against the rarity’s DC. If someone else with proficiency in Nature, Arcana, Alchemists Tools, or Herbalism Kit is helping you, you may roll with advantage. Once begun, you will have to roll this same check several more times before the brewing has completed. When the potion is completed, if you rolled more failures than successes, then the potion becomes unusable.

Time: You cannot pause the progress of making a potion and resume it at a later time. Each rarity specifies how many times you must tend to a potion (spread evenly throughout the brewing) and for how long you must spend for the interaction to count. Each time you tend to the potion, you must make another check against the potion’s DC.

  • Common: 12 Hours (1, 1 hr)
  • Uncommon: 3 days (3, 2 hrs)
  • Rare: 7 days (7, 2 hrs)
  • Very Rare: 3 weeks (21, 3 hrs)
  • Legendary: 6 months (24, 4 hrs)

Cost: Every potion requires some amount of supplies, with its rarity corresponding to the cost.

  • Common: 5 GP
  • Uncommon: 10 GP
  • Rare: 40 GP
  • Very Rare: 120 GP
  • Legendary: 500 GP

DC: Every potion has a DC that you must roll a Arcana check (with Alchemist Supplies) or a Nature Check (with Herbalism Kit), adding your proficiency to the roll (doubled if expertise), against.

  • Common: DC 8
  • Uncommon: DC 10
  • Rare: DC 13
  • Very Rare: DC 16
  • Legendary: DC 20

Learning how to make a potion: Every potion has some amount of studying that needs to be done in order to create it, even if you are copying instructions from a written source.

  • Common: 2 hours
  • Uncommon: 8 hours
  • Rare: 24 hours
  • Very Rare: 50 hours
  • Legendary: 120 hours
